title: The Deployer of Omaha: Greg Abel Finally Puts Berkshire's Cash Pile to Work
subtitle: Berkshire's cash hoard fell for the first time in 14 quarters, buybacks exploded to $4.53 billion, and the company became a net buyer of stocks for the first time in more than three years. The Oracle of Omaha era is yielding to the Deployer of Omaha.
summary: Berkshire Hathaway's Q2 2026 report, out Saturday August 8, delivered the shift investors have waited years for: the cash pile fell to $364.7 billion from a record of roughly $380 billion, the first meaningful drawdown in over three years. Operating earnings rose 16% to $12.98 billion, net income more than doubled to $25.67 billion, buybacks accelerated nearly twentyfold to $4.53 billion, and Berkshire became a net buyer of stocks for the first time in 14 quarters — roughly tripling its Alphabet stake to over $21 billion, taking positions in homebuilders DR Horton, Lennar, and NVR, and striking a $6.8 billion deal for Taylor Morrison. In Greg Abel's second quarter as CEO, the fortress balance sheet is finally being put to work.

bodyHtml:
The most important number in Berkshire Hathaway's second-quarter report was not the earnings, the buybacks, or the Alphabet stake. It was the cash pile. $364.7 billion — down from a record of roughly $380 billion — the first meaningful drawdown in more than three years. After a decade of critics howling about dead money, the hoard is finally moving. That is the story of this quarter, and it changes the way you have to think about Berkshire.

For years, the question hung over every Berkshire earnings call like a fog: why so much cash? Under Warren Buffett, the answer was patience — the elephant gun, held in reserve for the once-in-a-generation deal. The counterargument, repeated by short sellers and frustrated shareholders alike, was that a $380 billion pile earning a pittance was a permanent drag on returns. Greg Abel, in his second quarter as chief executive, has effectively settled the debate. The handoff was telegraphed for years, but the money tells you when it is really happening. The era of hoarding is over.

The operating engine, for its part, is humming. Operating earnings came in at $12.98 billion, up 16% from $11.16 billion a year earlier. Net income more than doubled to $25.67 billion, powered by $16.08 billion of investment gains as the stock portfolio appreciated. BNSF put up strong numbers, and the manufacturing, service, and retail operations were solid across the board. Foreign currency gains added a tailwind. This was not a quarter that needed excuses — it was a quarter that needed capital to deploy.

And deploy it did. Buybacks jumped to $4.53 billion in the quarter, against a paltry $235 million in Q1 — a nearly twentyfold acceleration. That matters. Berkshire has long repurchased its own shares, but rarely with this kind of urgency, and rarely with the stock trading near its highs. Combined with the new stock purchases, the message is unmistakable: management believes the market's best businesses, and its own shares, are worth buying right now.

Then there are the portfolio moves, which are the real headline. Berkshire was a net buyer of stocks for the first time in 14 quarters — the first time in more than three years that purchases exceeded sales. The biggest move: the Alphabet stake was roughly tripled to more than $21 billion. Berkshire also planted flags in homebuilders, taking positions in DR Horton, Lennar, and NVR, and struck a $6.8 billion deal to acquire Taylor Morrison. Apple, Alphabet, American Express, Bank of America, and Coca-Cola still anchor the top of the book, but the new buys say something about where Abel sees value: mega-cap tech at reasonable prices, and a housing market that is not going away. The positioning is coherent — and it is not what Buffett's Berkshire has looked like in years.

The scale of the machine is worth restating. Book value sits at roughly $748 billion of equity. Trailing twelve-month revenue is around $375 billion, and the market cap is about $1.125 trillion, with roughly 1.4 billion Class B shares outstanding — about 2.1 billion once Class A is included on an equivalent basis. On trailing earnings, the stock trades at about 15.5 times — not the bargain-bin valuation Berkshire skeptics keep waiting for, but hardly a bubble multiple for a company this size with this balance sheet.

Here is the bottom line. Berkshire under Abel is a different machine than Berkshire under Buffett — not because the philosophy changed, but because the moment did. Buffett remains chairman at 95, and his fingerprints are all over the culture, but this quarter carries Abel's signature: the cash is being put to work, the buybacks are aggressive, and the balance sheet is being repositioned in real time. The Oracle of Omaha is yielding to the Deployer of Omaha.

The risks are real. Deploying a fortress-sized cash pile into a market trading near its highs is a bet that the best businesses are still reasonably priced, and that bet can look foolish in a downturn. But the shift itself is the signal. For three and a half years, Berkshire sat. Now it is moving. Shareholders who spent a decade listening to cash-pile complaints finally have their answer — and it came with a receipt.
